mathprize-olympiad-2024-01.title: Two cyclic quadrilaterals and a power of a point
mathprize-olympiad-2024-01.body:
**No, it is impossible.** Suppose $AD,BE,CF$ concur at $X$; we derive $AB=AC$.

**Two circles.** Since $DB=DF$ and $F$ lies on segment $BA$, $\angle DFB=\angle DBF=\angle DBA=\angle DCA$. Hence $\angle AFD=180^\circ-\angle DFB=180^\circ-\angle ACD$. The points $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$ ($D$ is interior, so $AD$ separates $B$ and $C$, and $F$ is on $B$'s side), so $A,F,D,C$ are concyclic; call this circle $\omega_1$. Similarly $DE=DC$ gives $\angle DEC=\angle DCE=\angle DCA=\angle DBA$, so $\angle AED=180^\circ-\angle ABD$, and with $E,B$ on opposite sides of $AD$ the points $A,E,D,B$ are concyclic (circle $\omega_2$).

**Concurrency forces a third circle.** The cevians $BE$ and $CF$ meet at a point $X$ inside the triangle, lying inside the segments $BE$ and $CF$. Then $X$ is inside $\omega_1$ (on the chord $FC$) and inside $\omega_2$ (on the chord $BE$), and $X$ lies on line $AD$, which meets both circles at $A,D$. By the power of the point $X$,
$$XA\cdot XD=XF\cdot XC\quad\text{and}\quad XA\cdot XD=XB\cdot XE,$$
so $XB\cdot XE=XF\cdot XC$ and (with $X$ interior to both chords) $B,F,E,C$ are concyclic; call the circle $\omega$.

**$D$ is the centre of $\omega$.** $D$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BF$ ($DB=DF$) and of $EC$ ($DE=DC$); both pass through the centre of $\omega$. These two bisectors are perpendicular to the non-parallel lines $AB,AC$, so they meet in only one point; thus $D$ is the centre of $\omega$ and $DB=DF=DE=DC$.

**Conclusion.** Triangles $DBF$ and $DCE$ are isosceles with equal legs and equal base angles ($\angle DBF=\angle DCE$), hence congruent, so $BF=EC=:t$. By the power of the point $A$ with respect to $\omega$ (lines $AB$ and $AC$ meet $\omega$ at $F,B$ and $E,C$): $AF\cdot AB=AE\cdot AC$. With $c=AB$, $b=AC$: $(c-t)c=(b-t)b$, i.e. $(c-b)(c+b-t)=0$. Since $t<c$, we get $c=b$: $AB=AC$, contradicting scalene. So the lines are never concurrent. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2024-03.title: Heron's formula in coordinates
mathprize-olympiad-2024-03.body:
Let $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$. We must write $a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2$ as a sum of two integer squares. Place $A=(0,0)$, $B=(u,v)$, $C=(s,t)$ (a translation of the lattice triangle). Then
$$c^2=u^2+v^2,\quad b^2=s^2+t^2,\quad a^2=(u-s)^2+(v-t)^2$$
are integers, and $a^2+b^2+c^2=2\,(u^2+v^2+s^2+t^2-us-vt)$ is even. Let $k=|ut-vs|=2[ABC]$ (twice the area).

Heron's formula in the form $16[ABC]^2=2(a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2)-(a^4+b^4+c^4)$ gives $4k^2=2\sum a^2b^2-\sum a^4$. Adding $(a^2+b^2+c^2)^2=\sum a^4+2\sum a^2b^2$:
$$4k^2+(a^2+b^2+c^2)^2=4\,(a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2),$$
that is,
$$a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2=k^2+\left(\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}2\right)^2.$$
Both $k$ and $\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}2=u^2+v^2+s^2+t^2-us-vt$ are integers. Since $AB\cdot AC=cb$, $BC\cdot BA=ac$, $CA\cdot CB=ba$, the left side is exactly the required sum, so $m=k$, $n=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}2$ work. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2024-04.title: Counting, and a doubling construction
mathprize-olympiad-2024-04.body:
Condition (iii) says that the graph on the white cells (two cells adjacent if they share an edge) is connected and has no cycles (a cycle would give two paths between two of its vertices): it is a **tree**.

**Impossible when $n\equiv1\pmod3$.** Let there be $a$ white and $b$ black squares, $a+b=n^2$. Count the pairs of edge-adjacent squares in the grid: $2n(n-1)$ in total.
- Black-black pairs: $0$ by (ii).
- White-white pairs: $a-1$ (edges of a tree on $a$ vertices).
- White-black pairs: by (i) the only black squares on the boundary are the $4$ corners, which have $2$ neighbours; every other black square has $4$ neighbours. By (ii) all neighbours of a black square are white, so there are $4(b-4)+4\cdot2=4b-8$ such pairs.

Hence $(a-1)+(4b-8)=2n(n-1)$. With $a=n^2-b$ this gives $3b=n^2-2n+9$, so $3\mid n(n-2)$, i.e. $n\equiv0$ or $2\pmod3$. So for every $n\equiv1\pmod3$ (e.g. $4,7,10,\dots$) the task is impossible: infinitely many such $n$.

**Possible for infinitely many $n$.** *Base case $n=3$:* colour the four corners black and the other five cells white. The white cells form a plus shape, a tree; (i) and (ii) clearly hold.

*Doubling.* Suppose $\chi$ is a valid colouring of an $n\times n$ grid, $n\ge3$, with cells $(x,y)\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}^2$. Define a colouring $\chi'$ of the $(2n-1)\times(2n-1)$ grid, cells $(x,y)\in\{0,\dots,2n-2\}^2$:
- $(x,y)$ both odd: black;
- $x+y$ odd: white;
- $x,y$ both even: the colour of $\chi(x/2,\,y/2)$.

(i): a boundary cell has $x$ or $y$ in $\{0,2n-2\}$ (even), so it is not (odd,odd); if the other coordinate is odd it is white; if both are even it is a boundary cell of the old grid, which is black exactly at the four corners. (ii): every black cell has $x+y$ even, while adjacent cells have sums of different parity, so no two black cells are adjacent. (iii): call a cell with $x+y$ odd an *$A$-cell* and an (even,even) white cell a *$B$-cell*. $A$-cells are adjacent only to cells with even sum, and white cells with even sum are $B$-cells; $B$-cells have even sum so they are adjacent (among white cells) only to $A$-cells. An $A$-cell with ($x$ even, $y$ odd) has the two (even,even) neighbours $(x,y\pm1)$, which are the old cells $(\frac x2,\frac{y\mp1}2)$, vertically adjacent in the old grid; similarly for ($x$ odd, $y$ even). Its two even-even neighbours are old-adjacent cells, so by (ii) for $\chi$ they are not both black. Therefore the new white graph is: the old white tree with every edge subdivided once by the $A$-cell between its endpoints, plus an extra $A$-cell hanging as a leaf on each old white cell for every adjacent old black cell. A subdivided tree with leaves attached is again a tree. So $\chi'$ is valid.

Starting from $n=3$ and applying the map $n\mapsto2n-1$ repeatedly, we get valid colourings for $n=3,5,9,17,\dots=2^j+1$, infinitely many. ∎
